{{Short description|Topological space}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Ran space''' (or '''Ran's space''') of a [[topological space]] ''X'' is a topological space <math>\operatorname{Ran}(X)</math> whose underlying set is the set of all [[empty set|nonempty]] finite [[subset]]s of ''X'': for a [[metric space]] ''X'' the [[topological space|topology]] is induced by the [[Hausdorff distance]]. The notion is named after [[Ziv Ran]].

==Definition==
In general, the topology of the Ran space is generated by sets

: <math>\{ S \in \operatorname{Ran}(U_1 \cup \dots \cup U_m) \mid S \cap U_1 \ne \emptyset, \dots, S \cap U_m \ne \emptyset \}</math>

for any [[disjoint sets|disjoint]] [[open subset]]s <math>U_i \subset X, i = 1, ..., m</math>.

There is an analog of a Ran space for a [[Scheme (mathematics)|scheme]]:<ref>{{harvnb|Lurie|2014}}</ref> the '''Ran prestack''' of a [[quasi-projective scheme]] ''X'' over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] ''k'', denoted by <math>\operatorname{Ran}(X)</math>, is the [[category (mathematics)|category]] whose [[object (category theory)|objects]] are triples <math>(R, S, \mu)</math> consisting of a finitely generated [[algebra over a field|''k''-algebra]] ''R'', a nonempty set ''S'' and a map of sets <math>\mu: S \to X(R)</math>, and whose [[morphism]]s <math>(R, S, \mu) \to (R', S', \mu')</math> consist of a [[algebra homomorphism|''k''-algebra homomorphism]] <math>R \to R'</math> and a [[surjective]] map <math>S \to S'</math> that commutes with <math>\mu</math> and <math>\mu'</math>. Roughly, an ''R''-point of <math>\operatorname{Ran}(X)</math> is a nonempty finite set of ''R''-rational points of ''X'' "with labels" given by <math>\mu</math>. A theorem of Beilinson and Drinfeld continues to hold: <math>\operatorname{Ran}(X)</math> is [[acyclic complex|acyclic]] if ''X'' is connected.

==Properties==
A theorem of Beilinson and Drinfeld states that the Ran space of a [[Connected space|connected]] [[manifold]] is [[weakly contractible]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Beilinson|first1=Alexander|author-link1=Alexander Beilinson|last2=Drinfeld|first2=Vladimir|author-link2=Vladimir Drinfeld | title=Chiral algebras|url=https://archive.org/details/chiralalgebras00abei|url-access=limited|date=2004|publisher=American Mathematical Society|isbn=0-8218-3528-9|page=[https://archive.org/details/chiralalgebras00abei/page/n174 173]}}</ref>

== Topological chiral homology ==
If ''F'' is a [[cosheaf]] on the Ran space <math>\operatorname{Ran}(M)</math>, then its space of global sections is called the '''topological chiral homology''' of ''M'' with coefficients in ''F''. If ''A'' is, roughly, a family of commutative algebras parametrized by points in ''M'', then there is a [[factorizable sheaf]] associated to ''A''. Via this construction, one also obtains the topological chiral homology with coefficients in ''A''. The construction is a generalization of  [[Hochschild homology]].<ref>{{harvnb|Lurie|2017|loc=Theorem 5.5.3.11}}</ref>
<!--
== <math>\operatorname{Ran}_G(X)</math> and nonabelian Poincaré duality ==

If ''G'' is trivial, <math>\operatorname{Ran}_G(X) = \operatorname{Ran}(X)</math>

The basic idea is that one expects the forgetful functor <math>\operatorname{Ran}_G(X) \to \operatorname{Bun}_G(X)</math> to be a "homotopy equivalence"<ref>http://cgp.ibs.re.kr/~gabriel/notes/spr11/lurie_may_23.pdf {{Dead link|date=February 2022}}</ref>. Instead of making this precise, one can show it is a universal homological equivalence; i.e., induces homological equivalence after the base change. For characteristic zero, this was proved in Gaitsgory's paper.

The basic question to keep in mind is what is the [[homotopy type]] of <math>\operatorname{Bun}_G(X)</math>? The above thus gives an answer to this question. Since one thinks <math>\operatorname{Bun}_G(X)</math> is something global, while <math>\operatorname{Ran}_G(X)</math> is something local, this establishes the [[local-to-global principle]].

The idea may be also understood in terms of an analogy to "nonabelian Poincaré duality",<ref>{{harvnb|Lurie|2017|loc=Theorem 5.5.6.6.}}</ref> which says, in one formulation, the space of compactly supported sections of a "bundle" ''E'' on a manifold ''M'' is the [[topological chiral homology]] of ''E''.
